sentences.text: What Mr Iqbal told her, over about six weeks, in the wrong order and with a great many diversions, was this.
A swift lands to nest.
That is the only reason.
It builds under an eave or in a gap in a wall, it raises its young, and then it goes, and it does not come down again until the next nest.
A young swift leaves the nest and goes into the air and *does not land at all* until it is two, or three, or in some cases four years old.
It flies to Africa and it flies back and it does it again, and in between it never once stops.
It feeds in the air.
It drinks in the air, off the surface of a lake, without stopping.
It gathers material for the nest out of the air — bits of seed-fluff and feather that happen to be up there — because it cannot pick anything off the ground.
And it sleeps in the air.
It goes up at dusk, very high, two thousand metres, and it sleeps up there in the dark going round and round, and it comes down in the morning.
"That's not true," said Ada.

"It's extremely true," said Mr Iqbal, "and it took people a very long time to believe it, and if you'd like I'll show you where to check, because you should never take a fact off an old man who is enjoying himself." She checked.
It was true.
It was true in a way that made her cross.
She had been alive for eleven years on a planet where this was going on, and nobody had mentioned it.
It was not a secret.
It was not even difficult.
It was in a library book on the second shelf of a public library in a town with a retail park in it, and every adult she had ever met had been walking around not saying anything about it.
She put this to Mr Iqbal, with some heat.
"Yes," he said, delighted.

"Now you have found the actual problem, and the actual problem is not swifts." "What is it, then?" "People are given a small number of facts at school and they assume, quite reasonably, that if there had been better ones, those would have been included." He picked his tea back up.
"Nobody hid this from you, Ada.
It is simply that the world is a great deal stranger than the timetable has room for.
Most people never find that out.

The ones who do generally find it out by becoming annoyed about a bird, or a rock, or a number, and it is always an accident, and it is always small." She sat on the fire escape that evening in the warm and did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what got her.
A swift that has not nested has not landed.

If a bird had hatched under an eave the year Ada was born, and had gone into the air that August, and had not yet nested — and some of them do not, for three or four years — then that bird had been flying, continuously, without ever once putting its feet on anything, for as long as Ada had been alive.
Every night she had ever slept, it had been awake or asleep in the air.
Every single thing she had ever done, it had been flying.
She tried to make the thought hold still and it would not.
Every meal.
Every argument.
The whole of Year Three.
The fortnight her mother spent in hospital and the fortnight after it.
The night the boiler went and they all slept in the front room.

Every one of those had happened inside a stretch of time in which something weighing about as much as a bar of chocolate had been continuously airborne, over nine countries and two seas, without once stopping.
She could not decide whether that made her feel small or whether it made her feel slightly accompanied, and after about a week she stopped trying to decide and let it be both.
